title: A Mechanochemical Model of Plant Cell Expansion Regulation: Beyond the Acid Growth Hypothesis
content: The acid growth hypothesis explains the role of apoplastic acidification in auxin-induced plant cell expansion; however, it does not, on its own, explain the conditions under which this process develops into sustained, irreversible growth. Apoplastic acidification, cell-wall loosening, and the presence of turgor pressure do not invariably result in the same growth response. This indicates that cell expansion should be understood as an outcome of interactions among hormonal regulation, cell-wall mechanical properties, water availability, and metabolic status. Here, we propose an integrative mechanistic model of plant cell expansion regulation in which the transition to a growth-permissive functional state is a central component. Within this framework, apoplastic pH is not considered a sufficient determinant of growth in itself, but rather a regulatory factor that influences the capacity of the cell wall to undergo mechanical deformation. The realization of growth depends on the coordination of this process with turgor pressure, water transport, metabolic capacity, and mechanosensory feedback mechanisms. This approach integrates the regulation of plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases, cell-wall remodelling, the TOR–SnRK1 signalling axis, and Ca²⁺- and reactive oxygen species-mediated pathways into a unified conceptual framework. The model describes cell expansion as a sequence of transitions among restricted, growth-permissive, actively expanding, and reinforcing states. Rather than rejecting the acid growth hypothesis, it extends its explanatory scope by linking local changes in apoplastic pH and cell-wall mechanics to the regulation of water relations, metabolism, and sustained growth. The proposed framework provides a basis for experimental investigation of the mechanisms through which plant cells convert regulatory signals into irreversible expansion.
